answer.summary: Walter recommends focusing on one skill at a time, defining a concrete outcome and a time-bound practice plan, and doing strategy-related learning and practice every week. He also reverse-engineers strong examples to identify what makes them effective.

sections.heading: Set a goal and commit to a period of focused practice
sections.content: Choose one skill and set a timeframe—Walter suggests three or six months, depending on the behavior you want to change. Define an outcome that would demonstrate improvement; in another example, he aimed to ship successful experiments that increased activation within six months. He advises focusing on skills one at a time.

sections.heading: Build strategy learning and practice into every week
sections.content: For product strategy, Walter’s example is to spend six months doing something related to learning strategy every week: review another feature’s product strategy, dividing the work into manageable chunks (for example, one feature a week), and separately practice on your own product strategy. He suggests roughly three hours a week—perhaps an hour a day. The point is sustained practice, rather than reading an article and then returning to usual habits.

sections.heading: Study strong examples and keep developing
sections.content: When told to improve at strategy, Walter asks for examples of people doing it well or relevant artifacts, then reverse-engineers them: What questions do they answer, and how do they approach the work? He looks for patterns across examples, rather than assuming a particular format is the key. Six months is not a guarantee of mastery; he says you can continue for another six months or shift focus to another skill.
